parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the number multiplying $t$ inside the cosine and think about what that quantity tells you about how fast the oscillation repeats.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise the standard cosine form**
You have $V = 18\cos 40\pi t$. Beside you, remember the general form for any sinusoidal variation is $V = V_0 \cos \omega t$, where $V_0$ is the peak value and $\omega$ is the angular frequency in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$. Matching the two, $V_0 = 18\text{ V}$ and $\omega = 40\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Link angular frequency to period**
One full cycle is $2\pi$ radians of phase, so: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$ Put in the numbers: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{40\pi} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.050\text{ s}$$ That is the time for the cosine to repeat, as required.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Identify the peak value from the $V = 18\cos 40\pi t$ expression and recall how the effective heating voltage compares to the peak for a sinusoid.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Peak to r.m.s. for a sine wave**
The $18$ in front of the cosine is the maximum or peak voltage $V_0 = 18\text{ V}$. For a sinusoidal a.c., the r.m.s. value which gives the same heating power as d.c. is smaller than the peak by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$: $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{18}{\sqrt{2}} = 12.7\text{ V} \approx 13\text{ V}$$ Keep 2 significant figures to match the data.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the value of $\cos 40\pi t$ when $t = 0$ and what that means for the starting point of your sketch.
Hint 2: Use the period of $50\text{ ms}$ to work out how many complete cycles fit into the $0$ to $100\text{ ms}$ window and where the peaks and troughs will fall.
Hint 3: Check what the maximum positive and negative values of $V$ should be from the given equation and label them on the $V$-axis.
parts.proper_answer: Cosine curve of amplitude $18\text{ V}$ and period $50\text{ ms}$ for $0$ to $100\text{ ms}$: maxima $+18\text{ V}$ at $t = 0, 50, 100\text{ ms}$, minima $-18\text{ V}$ at $t = 25, 75\text{ ms}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Starting phase**
Because it is a cosine, at $t = 0$, $\cos 0 = 1$ so $V = +18\text{ V}$. You start at the top positive peak, not at zero like a sine curve. That is a common slip, so start high on the $y$-axis.

Step 2: **Period and shape**
From (a)(i) $T = 0.050\text{ s} = 50\text{ ms}$. From $0$ to $100\text{ ms}$ you get exactly two full cycles. Draw a smooth sinusoidal shape: $$V = 18\cos 40\pi t$$ It falls from $+18\text{ V}$ at $0$ to $0$ at $12.5\text{ ms}$, to $-18\text{ V}$ at $25\text{ ms}$, back to $0$ at $37.5\text{ ms}$, to $+18\text{ V}$ at $50\text{ ms}$, then repeats to $100\text{ ms}$.

Step 3: **Amplitude labels**
Mark the tops at $+18\text{ V}$ and bottoms at $-18\text{ V}$. Keep the curve symmetric about $V = 0$ with equal positive and negative halves. That shows correct amplitude, period and phase.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Compare the repeat time of the $P$ graph in Fig. 7.3 with the $50\text{ ms}$ period of the original $V$ and think about what type of rectification makes power pulsate twice as fast.
Hint 2: Read the peak power from Fig. 7.3 and recall that for a sinusoidal variation the average over time sits halfway between the maximum and minimum.
Hint 3: Combine your mean power with the r.m.s. voltage from (a)(ii) using the resistive heating relation to find the load resistance and hence the current.
parts.proper_answer: Any three from: rectification is full-wave; period of $P$ is $25\text{ ms}$ (frequency $40\text{ Hz}$); peak power $28\text{ W}$, mean power $14\text{ W}$; $R = 12\ \Omega$; peak current $1.6\text{ A}$ / r.m.s. current $1.1\text{ A}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot frequency doubling and full-wave rectification**
In Fig. 7.3 the power peaks repeat every $25\text{ ms}$, from $0$ to $25$ to $50$ to $75$ to $100\text{ ms}$. The original voltage period was $50\text{ ms}$. Power goes as $V^2/R$, so it is always positive and pulses twice per voltage cycle. The fact that there are no gaps and the frequency is doubled to: $$f = \frac{1}{25\times 10^{-3}} = 40\text{ Hz}$$ tells you both half-cycles are used. That is full-wave rectification.

Step 2: **Mean power from peak power**
Read the top of the $P$ curve: $P_{max} \approx 28\text{ W}$. Power varies between $0$ and $28\text{ W}$ sinusoidally squared, so its time average is half the peak: $$P_{mean} = \frac{P_{max}}{2} \approx 14\text{ W}$$ You can see this as the mid-line of the oscillation.

Step 3: **Resistance and current**
For a resistor, mean heating is set by r.m.s. values: $$P_{mean} = \frac{V_{r.m.s.}^2}{R}$$ Using $V_{r.m.s.} \approx 12.7\text{ V}$ and $P_{mean} \approx 14\text{ W}$: $$R = \frac{(12.7)^2}{14} \approx 12\ \Omega$$ Then peak current follows from peak voltage: $$I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R} = \frac{18}{12} = 1.5\text{ - }1.6\text{ A}$$ depending on rounding, and r.m.s. current $I_{r.m.s.} = I_0/\sqrt{2} \approx 1.1\text{ A}$. Any three valid qualitative or quantitative statements earn credit.
